headline: Mojo 1.0 open-sourced, targets high-performance AI development alongside Python
summary: Mojo 1.0 is now open-source, offering Python-like syntax with advanced features for high-performance AI. It aims to complement, rather than replace, Python in critical AI development.
details: Mojo, a new programming language focused on high-performance computing and AI workloads, has reached version 1.0 and is now open-source under Apache 2.0. It aims to bring Python-like syntax to performance-critical tasks, especially on GPUs and accelerators.

Python became the default for much AI development due to its ease of use, despite performance limitations for low-level hardware. Mojo addresses this by offering a blend of Python's familiarity with systems-oriented capabilities.

The language features static typing, memory safety, and compile-time programming, enabling direct control over CPU, GPU, and accelerator hardware. This allows developers to optimize code closer to the metal without abandoning a Python-like experience.

Crucially, Mojo supports Python interoperability, meaning developers can integrate it into existing Python projects. This allows Python to continue dominating high-level AI ecosystems while Mojo handles the underlying performance-critical code.

Modular, the company behind Mojo, has been building tooling specifically for AI-assisted GPU kernel development. This positions Mojo uniquely in a landscape where AI coding agents are increasingly involved in software creation.

The co-existence model suggests Python will manage application logic and AI orchestration, with Mojo stepping in where compiled performance and hardware control are paramount. This makes Mojo a serious contender for long-term evaluation in the AI space.

headline_marked: [[Authentic Carnival Cruise Line email]] delivered malware to customers
headline: Authentic Carnival Cruise Line email delivered malware to customers
summary: A lapsed promotional domain, still linked from legitimate booking confirmations, was re-registered by an attacker and used to route real visitors to scareware and backdoors.
details: Customers clicking links in genuine Carnival Cruise Line booking confirmation emails were redirected to malware. The emails passed all authentication checks (SPF, DKIM, DMARC), appearing fully legitimate.

The vulnerability stemmed from a promotional domain that Carnival had allowed to lapse. This domain was subsequently re-registered by a malicious actor and integrated into a sophisticated redirection network.

This network employed device-aware cloaking: automated scanners and datacenter IPs received a benign parking page, while real browsers on home connections were served scareware, browser hijackers, and even backdoor installers.
Carnival re-acquired the lapsed domain on August 26th, 2026, effectively neutralizing this specific malware delivery vector. The issue was active for months before resolution.

Researchers had previously documented the redirection technique (PseudoTDS) and malware family (PhantomJack). However, this incident marked a new delivery path, leveraging authenticated marketing emails instead of mistyped domains.
The incident highlights how sophisticated attackers can exploit overlooked digital assets and advanced cloaking to bypass traditional security checks and deliver payloads to unsuspecting users.
